terms.definition: The tendency for a language model's ability to use relevant information reliably to decline as the amount of context grows, even when the needed information remains inside the context window.
terms.example: The answer got worse after we loaded the entire archive into the prompt, a sign of context rot rather than a missing context window.

terms.definition: The ability of a language model to accept and work with unusually large amounts of input in a single context window.
terms.example: The long-context model could take the full contract set at once, although careful retrieval was still useful.

terms.definition: A search method that compares vector representations of data to find items that are close to a query in embedding space.
terms.example: The application used vector search to find documents that were semantically related to the question.

terms.definition: A search method that returns items most similar to a query according to a chosen distance or similarity measure.
terms.example: Similarity search returned passages whose embeddings were closest to the user's query.

terms.definition: A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction, calculated from the cosine of the angle between them.
terms.example: The retrieval system used cosine similarity to rank document embeddings against the query embedding.

terms.definition: A structured representation of entities and the relationships between them, typically modeled as connected nodes and edges.
terms.example: The assistant used a knowledge graph to connect the project, client, document, and equipment records.

terms.definition: An organized collection of information that a system can store, retrieve, or use as a source of reference knowledge.
terms.example: The support assistant retrieves policy details from the company's internal knowledge base before answering.

terms.definition: A retrieval-augmented generation approach in which one or more AI agents actively decide how, when, and where to retrieve information as part of a multi-step workflow.
terms.example: The agentic RAG system searched several sources, evaluated the results, and ran a second retrieval before answering.

terms.definition: A retrieval-augmented generation approach that uses graph-structured information, often including a knowledge graph and graph-derived summaries, to retrieve context for a language model.
terms.example: Graph RAG helped answer questions that depended on relationships spread across many documents rather than one matching passage.

context-rot.origin: Context rot is a recent label for a long-context failure pattern in which model performance becomes less reliable as the amount of input grows. Chroma's July 2025 technical report used the phrase as its title, and Anthropic later described it as a concept revealed by long-context evaluation.

firstKnownUse.note: Chroma's technical report is a clear documented naming event for the phrase in current LLM usage; AILex does not claim it proves the absolute first informal use.

history.event: Chroma published ‘Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance,’ reporting that model reliability often degrades as input length grows.
Anthropic discussed context rot while explaining why context should be treated as a finite resource with diminishing returns.

sources.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
Effective context engineering for AI agents

long-context.origin: Long context is a descriptive technical category rather than a single coined term. It became especially prominent as language-model context windows expanded and developers began treating very large input capacity as a distinct model capability.

history.event: Anthropic described context as a finite resource and discussed performance degradation as token counts grow, highlighting the distinction between large capacity and reliable use of that capacity.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

vector-search.origin: Vector search grows from established nearest-neighbor and information-retrieval techniques. In modern AI systems, it commonly refers to searching embeddings or other numerical vector representations for nearby items.

similarity-search.origin: Similarity search is an established information-retrieval and nearest-neighbor concept rather than a generative-AI coinage. Modern embedding systems use it to retrieve vectors that are close according to a distance or similarity metric.

cosine-similarity.origin: Cosine similarity is an established mathematical and information-retrieval measure that predates modern AI. It became especially common in text retrieval and embedding systems because it compares vector direction rather than raw magnitude.

history.event: Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze documented cosine scoring in vector-space information retrieval, reflecting its established use for comparing text representations.

sources.title: Pairwise metrics, Affinities and Kernels — Cosine similarity

knowledge-graph.origin: Knowledge graphs descend from older semantic-network and graph-based knowledge-representation research. The modern label became widely associated with large-scale entity-and-relationship representations, especially after Google's 2012 Knowledge Graph launch.

history.event: Google introduced the Knowledge Graph as a way to represent real-world things and their relationships for search.

sources.title: Introducing the Knowledge Graph: things, not strings

knowledge-base.origin: Knowledge base is a long-established computing and knowledge-management term for an organized body of information intended for retrieval or reasoning. Generative-AI systems often use knowledge bases as external sources for RAG and grounding.

agentic-rag.origin: Agentic RAG extends retrieval-augmented generation by giving AI agents responsibility for parts of the retrieval process, such as query routing, planning, source selection, tool use, and iterative retrieval. The label emerged as agentic AI and RAG architectures converged in the mid-2020s.

history.event: IBM described agentic RAG as the use of AI agents to facilitate RAG and highlighted planning, routing, tool use, and retrieval across multiple sources.

graph-rag.origin: Graph RAG applies graph structures to retrieval-augmented generation. Microsoft Research's GraphRAG project made the label prominent in 2024 by combining LLM-derived knowledge graphs, graph analysis, community summaries, and retrieval for complex questions over private text corpora.

firstKnownUse.note: Microsoft Research publicly used GraphRAG in a project post on this date; AILex treats this as a documented introduction event for the named approach, not proof of the absolute first graph-based RAG work.

history.event: Microsoft Research published ‘GraphRAG: Unlocking LLM discovery on narrative private data.’
Microsoft released GraphRAG on GitHub as a graph-based RAG research system.
